A 40-ton red harvest does not need a 40-ton tank. It needs eleven of the right ones.

The most expensive sizing mistake in a cellar is buying fermentation capacity by annual volume instead of by lot. You end up blending two blocks you meant to keep apart, or filling a 10,000 L tank to a third and fighting oxygen all winter.

The working rule: about 1,000 litres of red fermenter per ton of fruit, about 700 litres of white tank per ton of juice, then round up to the next catalogue size. Tanks run 500 to 20,000 L, from around $3,400.

Your quote says 50 hL, 3,000 kg/h, DN50, 2 bar, 400V. Here is what that costs you if you read it wrong.

50 hL is 5,000 litres — but ask whether that is usable or gross, because only one of them holds wine. 3,000 kg/h is about 3.3 tons an hour, measured on clean dry fruit. DN50 is a 2-inch line. And 400V/50Hz is European three-phase; a US site needs 60Hz, which is not always a simple swap.

Most of the best winery equipment is Italian or French. The quote arrives in units your cellar does not use. Send us one and we will translate it.

Most wineries shopping for crossflow do not need crossflow yet.

If you are polishing clean wine before the filler, plates and cartridges do it for a fraction of the capital. If you are pushing heavy lees, a dedicated lees filter protects the membranes you just paid for. Crossflow earns its money on bulk, turbid, post-ferment wine you want off in a single pass with almost no oxygen pickup.

Then the only sum that matters: litres to filter ÷ hours you will actually run. 20,000 L in a ten-hour day is 2,000 L/hr minimum — and rated throughput is measured on clean wine, so buy a step up.

A 6,000 bottle-per-hour line empties a 10,000-case winery in about twenty hours.

Which means the line you are pricing runs for two days a year. Buy for a day you will never have and you have financed steel that sits still for 363 of them.

Bottles per hour should map to your annual volume and the bottling window you actually have. Lines run 1,000 to 6,000 BPH, from around $18,500.

Your crusher-destemmer is sized by your worst morning, not your annual tonnage.

Three blocks arrive at once, the fruit is warming on the pad, and the machine that coped fine all season becomes the bottleneck that decides your vintage.

Take your peak-day intake, divide by the hours you actually have, then buy a step up — rated throughput is measured on clean, dry, hand-picked fruit, not on a rainy pick full of MOG. Machines run 1 to 30 tons an hour, from around $7,800.

The honest answer to “how many bottles per hour do I need” is usually lower than the first guess.

Speed you never use is financed steel standing still. A 5,000-case winery running a 2,000 BPH line is done in four days — the 6,000 BPH machine finishes sooner and costs considerably more.

Map BPH to your annual volume and the window you actually have. We show throughput next to price so the trade-off is visible before anyone quotes you.

If you are pricing a press in July, the calendar has already decided for you.

Most of the world's best winery equipment is built in Italy and France, and both largely close in August. On top of the build sits freight, customs and commissioning — the machine has to be running before the fruit lands, not merely delivered.

Crusher-destemmers run 8–12 weeks, presses 12–16, tanks 10–14, bottling lines 16–24. Tell us your target vintage and we will tell you plainly what can still make it.

You do not need 316L everywhere. You do need it somewhere — and a bad weld cancels either grade.

304 is the food-grade workhorse and meaningfully cheaper: right for most tank bodies in a normal cellar. 316L earns its premium where chlorides and low pH live — coastal air, hard water, aggressive sanitation. The “L” is low carbon, which protects the corrosion resistance right at the welds.

Ask which surfaces are which, whether the interior welds were back-purged and passivated, and whether the material certs exist. A premium grade on a rough weld is still a rough weld.

Used winery equipment can cut capital outlay 40–60%. The risk is real, and it is not spread evenly.

A used storage tank is an easy yes. A used press in the middle of your crush is a different question. The honest test is what happens if it fails on the worst possible day: if nothing stops, buy used; if the vintage stops, buy vetted.

We will tell you which category a machine falls into before you spend anything — including when the answer is buy it used and keep the money.

The cheap press does not fail. It just retires early, in the middle of your harvest.

Buying on the lowest quote means discovering cycle time later, usually on the morning the crush pad backs up. Buying on the working number means starting from your peak tonnage, comparing cycle time rather than capacity, and checking the membrane, the drainage and whether parts still exist.

Same manufacturers either way. We just put the number that decides your day next to the number on the quote.

Most oxidation problems people blame on the wine start in the transfer line.

Work out the flow you need — tank volume divided by the time you want it to take — then check the spec nobody quotes: shear. A pump fast enough on paper that whips air into the must costs you more than the hour it saved.

We list flow, shear behaviour and the sanitary fittings side by side, from vetted European makers.

Every machine in your cellar is judged in those six weeks. Which is exactly why lead time, parts availability and service response should outrank sticker price — a bargain that cannot be repaired in September is not a bargain.
